newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: ASIAN EXOTICS - Regionals under siege.
newsitem.headline: ASIAN EXOTICS - Regionals under siege.

text.p: * Regional currencies back on roller coaster ride as uncertainty following effective devaluation of Philippine peso spreads to others.
* Malaysian ringgit plummets to 16-month low amid Bank Negara's apparent inaction.
* Thai central bank intervenes to stem baht's fall in domestic markets.
* Indonesian rupiah recovers from early plunge. Last week's band widening fails to support currency.
* Singapore dollar succumbs to regional pressure but downside limited due to sound fundamentals and country's huge forex reserves.
Southeast Asian currencies were hit by waves of selling on Monday as uncertainty following the Philippine peso's effective devaluation last week spread like wildfire through the region.
In Malaysia, the ringgit fell to a 16-month low of 2.5500 to the dollar in early trade amid Bank Negara Malaysia's failure to intervene aggressively, dealers said.
The ringgit was quoted at 2.5375/95 to the dollar at 0400 GMT against 2.5042/52 at its Kuala Lumpur close on Friday.
"The market is quoting 30 to 50 pips in dollar/ringgit. It's crazy," a European bank dealer in Singapore said.
"Because of the story of the Philippine peso, which they devalued last week, the market is expecting the ringgit and rupiah to follow suit," she said.

Another European bank dealer in Singapore said Bank Negara was heard to have sold dollars around the 2.5500 ringgit level. "But I think Negara was in just to slow down the fall rather than stop the flow," he said.
Dealers said the market was still long of dollars, leaving room for the ringgit to head lower.
They said Bank Negara may be allowing market forces to dictate the spot's value rather than defending the ringgit aggressively in the face of heavy selling interest.
The Malaysian central bank spent over $1 billion to support the ringgit last week.
In Indonesia, the rupiah rebounded from its early lows as offshore players began unloading dollars.
Dealers said offshore players seemed to be trying to cash out from the market after they drove the rupiah to a low of 2,469.0 on Monday morning.
"I think some feel that the rupiah is low enough for a buy back, reversing the market trend," a local bank dealer in Jakarta said.

But another local bank dealer said the rupiah buying was initiated by some state banks and followed through by offshore players, driving the rupiah to a high of 2,445 before operators bought some dollars back.
The rupiah was quoted at 2,453.0/58.0 at 0400 GMT against an opening 2,451.0/55.0.

"Bank Indonesia (BI)'s band widening last week is not helping to strengthen the rupiah. With BI having the lowest reserves, the rupiah will be the next currency to attack," a Singapore-based dealer said.

The central bank widened its intervention band to 12 percent from eight percent last Friday, in what was seen as a move to pre-empt possible turbulence in the rupiah after speculative attacks on the peso and baht.
A U.S. bank dealer in Jakarta said offshore operators continued to accumulate rupiah in the swap market, bracing for a possible money market liquidity squeeze by the central bank.
Six-month swaps were at around 120/130 points.
But money market dealers said there was no such indication because rupiah liquidity was abundant in the market, with overnight rates falling to 13.0 percent from 19.5 percent.

In the Philippines, the peso fell to a low of 29.75 to the dollar in thin trade as banks remained wary after the central bank's move on Friday to allow the peso-dollar rate to trade within a wider band.
Volume was a light nine million dollars after two-and-a-half hours of trading on Monday.
The central Bank of Thailand (BOT) intervened to stem the baht's fall in domestic markets, selling dollars at the 30.75-30.80 baht level, dealers said.
"The central bank intervened through a small local bank by selling the dollar at around 30.75-30.80," a European bank dealer in Bangkok said.
A BOT spokeswoman declined to say whether the central bank had intervened in the market.
Commercial dollar demand and lingering jitters from the peso slide pushed the baht to new lows.
The currency was quoted at 30.500/30.800 to the dollar in the domestic market at 0400 GMT, after the intervention, against 30.00/30.60 late on Friday.
"The amount of intervention was insignificant. But it capped the baht at around 30.80," the dealer said.
Even the typically stoic Singapore dollar came under some pressure, falling to a low of 1.4440 against its U.S. counterpart compared with an opening of around 1.4410.
But the currency later recovered ground and dealers said it should be largely immune from the regional turmoil due to sound economic fundamentals and Singapore's huge reserves.
"The MAS (Monetary Authority of Singapore) has over US$60 billion in the bank and you can't short the currency," one trader noted.
-- Syed Azman in Kuala Lumpur (603-206 2323), Mantik Kusjanto in Jakarta (6221 384-6364), Anuchit Nguyen in Bangkok (662) 652-0642, and Sonali Desai in Singapore (65-8703090)
